summary: The SIP event notification framework lets users subscribe to changes in a resource but lacks a way to filter them. This document describes what subscribers do to attach filtering rules to a subscription, how responses and filtered notifications are handled, and how notifiers behave. It was later updated by RFC 6665.

eli5.summary: Instead of getting a text every time anything changes, you tell the sender which changes you care about. This explains how to set that up and how the sender follows it.

subtitle: How SIP subscribers attach filters to a subscription and how notifiers and list servers must honor them.

tldr.problem: The SIP event notification framework lets a user subscribe to changes in a resource but has no way to limit what a notification contains or when it is sent, which hurts devices with low bandwidth and limited battery.
tldr.mechanism: The subscriber puts an XML filter in the SUBSCRIBE body. The notifier applies the what part to choose the content and the trigger part to decide when to notify, and a resource list server routes filters to the right back-end subscriptions.
tldr.outcome: It defines the client, list server and notifier behaviour, error handling and security limits. It was later updated by RFC 6665.

today: RFC 4660 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6665. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Filter Notifications
sections.content:
SIP event notification (RFC 3265) lets a subscriber ask a notifier to send a NOTIFY when a resource changes. Normally the notification carries the full state of the resource the subscriber is allowed to see.

Filtering controls what a notification contains and, optionally, when it is sent. The RFC expects it to be especially valuable for mobile wireless devices, which tend to have high latency, low bandwidth, small displays and limited battery power. It warns that filtering adds computational burden at the notifier. The XML format of the filter itself is in RFC 4661; this RFC describes the behaviour. It assumes every NOTIFY body is an XML document.
sections.eli5: If your phone buzzed for every tiny change, the battery would die. Filtering lets you say, only tell me about the changes I care about.

sections.title: What the Subscriber Does
sections.content:
The filter goes in the body of the SUBSCRIBE with the content type application/simple-filter+xml, which compliant entities MUST support. It can alternatively be uploaded by means outside the RFC. A SUBSCRIBE with no body asks for no filter, so the notifier uses its own policy. Honouring a filter is at the notifier's discretion and may depend on local policy.

Several <filter> elements may appear in one request, but each filter must identify a unique resource or domain. If a filter has no uri, it applies to the resource in the Request-URI. A filter can also use a domain attribute, and a resource-specific filter overrides a domain filter. A filter can be disabled and re-enabled through the enabled attribute.

Inside an existing dialog, filters persist. A new SUBSCRIBE with no filter keeps the current ones. Sending the same filter ID replaces a filter, remove="true" deletes it, and changing the ID while keeping the resource URI is an error, because it looks like two filters for one resource.

Responses: a 200 means the subscription and filter are accepted. A 202 means the subscription was understood but the filter is not yet accepted, and acceptance may come in a later NOTIFY. A 415 means the filter content type is not understood, and a 488 means it was understood but some part was not understood or not accepted.
sections.eli5: You write down your wish list, send it with your request, and can edit or cross out items later. The sender answers yes, maybe-later, or sorry-I-do-not-get-this.

sections.title: Resource List Servers and Filters
sections.content:
A Resource List Server (RLS) takes one subscription to a list and fans it out to many resources. When a filter has no URI, or its URI matches the Request-URI, the RLS applies it to all notifications it sends for that subscription.

If a filter names one resource that belongs to the list, the RLS extracts just that filter and puts it in the SUBSCRIBE it sends to that resource. If the named resource is outside the RLS's administrative control, the filter is propagated to all the fanned-out subscriptions, since a sub-list may live in another domain. If the resource is under the RLS's control but not on the list, the filter is not propagated, and the RLS must apply it itself to notifications it receives.

A filter addressed to a domain is not applied by the RLS at all. The RLS MUST forward it with every fanned-out subscription. If two filters target the same resource or domain, the RLS MUST reject the request with a 488.
sections.eli5: A list server is like a teacher passing a note to each student. It hands each student only the part of your note that is about them, and keeps the rest.

sections.title: What the Notifier Does
sections.content:
The notifier returns 415 if it does not understand the filter content type, and rejects duplicate filters for the same resource or domain with 488. It SHOULD keep the filter for as long as the subscription lasts. A notifier that is not responsible for a filter's domain MUST ignore it.

What gets sent depends on the filter. With only a <what> element, the notifier sends the requested state whenever the resource changes. With only a <trigger>, it sends all state whenever a change matches the trigger. With both, it sends the requested state when a change matches the trigger. If any one of several triggers is satisfied, a NOTIFY SHOULD be generated. A disabled filter means the same as no filter. Re-enabling one makes the notifier act as if it had just been placed.

The first NOTIFY after a 2xx response MUST be populated according to <what>, and trigger values are ignored for it. If processing takes too long, the body may be empty or a pre-configured value. If filtering leaves nothing, the body MUST be empty. The result MUST be well-formed and valid, so the notifier MUST add back any mandatory elements and attributes the filter removed.

If a filter asks for things the subscriber is not authorized to see, notifier policy decides. It is RECOMMENDED that the notifier just ignore those parts of the filter.
sections.eli5: The sender sorts your wish list into what to tell you and when. If you ask for something you are not allowed to know, the sender quietly skips it.

sections.title: Errors and XML Validity
sections.content:
If the filter does not match the filter XML schema, the notifier rejects the SUBSCRIBE with a 488, and a Warning header field may explain why. If a 202 was already sent and the bad filter is found later, a NOTIFY with subscription-state terminated is sent, and the new event-reason-value badfilter MAY be included. An erroneous expression leads the notifier to either ignore the filter or end the subscription. An empty <what> or <trigger> is treated as if it were not there.

The subscriber MUST send well-formed, valid XML and MUST NOT add extension elements unless it has the extension schema. The notifier MAY validate against the schemas it has.
sections.eli5: If your wish list is written wrong, the sender says no. If they only notice later, they tell you the subscription has ended and say the filter was bad.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Filters change how a request is handled, so messages carrying them should be authenticated and authorized. The RFC points to SIP Digest authentication. Because filter evaluation costs computation, a user could try to overload a server with large filters. The server can limit how many <what>, <changed>, <added> and <removed> elements are allowed, and a default limit of 40 is RECOMMENDED.

Filters can reveal a user agent's capabilities, so they SHOULD be encrypted with SIP S/MIME if sensitive. An RLS must not forward a filter for a resource under its control but not on the list, since that would leak information about the user's lists. Subscribers should also remember that a filtered view can mislead: if you only ask to hear about a change to "open", you may think a resource is still open long after it closed.
sections.eli5: The sender should check who you are before obeying your list. It may also refuse a list that is ridiculously long, and you should remember that if you only ask to hear good news, you might miss the bad.

items.label: Accepted
items.desc: Subscription, authorization and filter accepted; NOTIFY follows immediately.

items.label: Understood
items.desc: Subscription understood but filter not yet accepted; acceptance may come in a later NOTIFY.

items.label: Not acceptable
items.desc: Filter understood but some aspect not understood or not accepted, for example duplicate filters for one resource.
